Some of the bosses in this game are the best in Fromsoft history, such as the final boss.  I also love love love love love the enhanced Adel; he seems super annoying and obnoxious at first, but once you learn his fight (which isn't too hard imo) he's some of the most fun I've had in a Souls game.  But, of course, this game still has a terrible boss: Maris.  God awful design, fight wise

And the idea to bring in bosses from other Fromsoft Souls games was a stroke of genius, and now I will be waiting for them to add Gael to the game

Mix all of this with Souls / ER combat mechanics and it's just... chef's kiss.  I'm truly in love

It's very hard to decide how good this game is.

On one hand, most of the minibosses feel pretty lazy, the map barely changes throughout runs and there's only 1 main map which feels pretty damn repetitive overtime, even if your spawn changes and things get shuffled around a little bit, the good/affordable skins are only available in the postgame, and the game is short as hell, I beat it all in like, 11 hours.

On the other hand, I love what they changed/added with the combat system, the movement system, and the main bosses are just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome and are all huge spectacles with some of the best music fromsoft has ever cooked up.

So, the highs are high, and the lows aren't that low, but noticable. I'd say the price for this game is pretty reasonable with how good it is, about a 6.5/10 imo. Good, but not FromSoft's next big thing kinda good. Definitely needs some work, but can still be fun as is

Wanted to 100% before I gave the review:

Been running solo with Randies (because none of my friends play), and it’s honestly a joy. The time-honored FromSoft tradition of carrying strangers through near-impossible odds is alive and well. I get the gripes about if you don't have friends don't play, but I sincerely disagree.

The core loop is tight and satisfying: one part Elden Ring, one part Monster Hunter, with a dash of Battle Royale pacing. Each run spans two in-game days, with a shrinking safe zone pushing you toward a boss at the end of each. Survive that? Congrats, now face the final boss on day three.

Each character plays wildly different, and no two runs feel the same. It’s just enough like the original to feel familiar, but different enough to feel fresh. There's true tank support toons that don't do any DPS. Pure DPS monster toons that are made of glass. A parry toon that plays like Sekiro if you're into that - and so much more. On top of that, as you play the toons more you unlock these little memory fragments that further dive into their each respective lore, and unlock side quests/char specific items.

They've also since added ultra versions of certain bosses that rotate weekly and are an absolute blast to fight. they reward you with special currency to obtain better items and other rewards purchasable with the regular currency.

Would recommend. Every run is a mess, and every mess is worth it.
There are some definite technical issues and QOL issues that fromsoft needs to fix, but overall the game slaps. Def recommend playing with at least 1 friend.

Taking the meat and guts of Elden Ring and trying to reformat it into a roguelike structure is an inherently worrisome prospect. The original game heavily emphasizes exploration, immersion, and experimentation, allowing the player to approach their numerous options at any given point at a pace and order that they are comfortable with. Roguelikes of the variety that Nightreign is aiming for are more directly oriented toward building yourself up as fast and efficiently as possible, disregarding or abandoning routes that do not offer the possibility of powerful long-term gains. Unfortunately, I find that the experience of Elden Ring, a game I love, weighs too heavily in my mind when I'm faced with how Nightreign's changes grind against it.

I find that the moment-to-moment experience of Nightreign feeling so similar to the original game (albeit with some enhancements that I have genuinely enjoyed, like character skills and passives) ends up working against the roguelike structure. Nearly every run I've done in this game led to at least one moment of extreme frustration as my intended routing was interrupted by the encroaching "Tide of Night" (aka the storm in Fortnite) blocking off what could have been a valuable checkpoint. or just an interesting new area yet to be explored (such as the Shifting Land events, or many of the required encounters needed to complete Remembrances). However, the odds of a location on the map providing a weapon, item, or buff that is valuable is still based on luck regardless, so there will often be expeditions where the RNG leads to me and my friends feeling severely unprepared despite our best efforts. These issues then compound on one another at the third day, when the encounter with the bosses can be derailed as quickly as any of the original boss fights in Elden Ring, resulting in having to redo the entire experience in order to try for another attempt.

Frankly, I hoped we had moved past boss runbacks in Souls games after Elden Ring, yet Nightreign seems keen to circulate its entire structure around it. If that idea makes you shudder at the thought like it did for me when the game was announced, then I am sorry to say that this game does nothing to make it more exciting than it sounds. The rewards of Murk (the game's long-term currency, used for minor upgrades and some very impressive cosmetics) and relics to alter your runs in various ways soon become paltry offerings once you have a decent build put together on your characters of choice...especially when some of the most coveted skins, those of existing characters in previous Souls games, remained locked behind defeating the final boss first.

The result of all of these factors is that the minute-to-minute experience of Nightreign starts to feel extremely stressful, frantic, and constrained, where your ability to confidently defeat a Nightlord is dictated by your ability to complete a very specific set of objectives in an expedited manner...if those objectives even spawn at all. The difference between an advantaged or heavily disadvantaged run on one particular boss is entirely determined by whether or not a specific camp spawns granting access to weapons that use his weakness, which you'll know immediately upon beginning your hunt. These difficulties simply do not exist in the original Elden Ring, whose fans Nightreign seems primarily keen to entice to play this new entry. If that is the intention, then others like myself will likely be put off by how regimented the experience quickly becomes.

Ultimately, most runs result in the same formula of attacking small forts and Evergaol's at the beginning of Day 1, then closing in on the central castle or a camp holding the boss's weakness until night falls and the first major boss rears its head. Day 2 typically entails resuming attacking the central castle, engaging with one of the Shifting Earth areas that jolt a bit of variety into the experience, or confronting one of the camps corrupted by Invaders. After the Night 2 boss is confronted, should you not have a proper arsenal or adequate levels to face the boss, you are faced with the loathsome prospect of having to repeat the entire endeavor (35-45 minutes on average for me), with even odds as to whether you will have better luck on the next series of encounters and loot drops. This sounds like a common description of the typical roguelike experience, but these features of the overall gameplay that Nightreign is built around are the same ones that the original Elden Ring, and the entire Souls franchise, have been moving away from for years.

As far back as Dark Souls, if you knew what you were doing, you could truly conquer the standard Souls game with enough skill. What this allowed for is for the experience of repeated playthroughs to be diversified by experimentation with new builds or challenge runs, emphasized by boss souls offering one of two options requiring multiple NG+ runs or new characters to fully realize the available features. Those obstructions worked to the game's inherent benefit, as rerunning previous Souls games offers a wealth of diverse experiences in the game world itself, especially in deviating questlines. When Elden Ring released, a key part of its universal acclaim was its seeming perfection of the model that Fromsoft has been cultivating all this time, Trying to do something different in a new entry is commendable, but attempting to tear up and graft the perfected Souls-like experience into an overdone, ill-fitting roguelike structure results in far too many gears turning against one another to make my overall engagement with Nightreign enjoyable in hindsight, save for a few peaks like the Nightlord bosses and Remembrance questlines impeded by far too many hurdles to even attempt.

Do not play this game for a fun new spin on the Souls-like experience. It certainly is a "new spin," but Nightreign will hopefully serve as a valuable lesson for what works and what doesn't when meshed together across video game genres.
